13.	Financial conditions during the past year have reflected the continued easy money position at home, the modest revival in business and the disturbances due to repeated crises abroad. Both our stock and bond markets have followed the general trend of the American markets, though they show a somewhat smaller net upward movement. Long term interest rates, indicated in the table below by the yield on dominion bonds, averaged lower than in any previous fiscal year. Short term rates were lower on the average than in preceding years, though occasional months have shown higher rates.
In the field of foreign exchange the year was marked by a decline of nearly all currencies relative to the American dollar. The premium on the American dollar in terms of the Canadian dollar rose during the spring and summer of 1938 to an average of about 1 per cent in June, and since that time has fluctuated between 0-3 per cent and 1 per cent in terms of monthly averages. Sterling exchange has declined from about S5.00 in March, 1938, a year ago, to about S4-70 recently.
Total net new bond issues in 1938 were approximately SI 19 million, compared with S60 million in 1937, the increase being accounted for by Dominion and Canadian National Railway issues. As in 1937 there was a small net retirement of corporation bonds. The amount of bonds payable in foreign currencies retired in 1938 was $69 million compared with $121 million in 1937, and S194 million in 1936. It is estimated that there was a total net export of capital amounting to about S160 million, but that there was a net sale of securities to foreigners of about S29 million, mainly in the form of Canadian common and preferred stocks.
Between March, 1938, and March, 1939, the Bank of Canada increased its total reserves by nearly 14 per cent. It increased its holdings of gold substantially, but reduced its holdings of securities by a smaller amount. The result was an increase in the cash reserves of the chartered banks of S14 million. Mr. Speaker, I am sure I but express the view of every hon. member of this house when I indicate to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) my gratification at his having recovered in health to such an extent as to be able to discharge this day and on this occasion so arduous a task, and do it so well. I should like also to congratulate the minister on the new system which he inaugurated to-day, which I believe is an adaptation of a combination of the systems in vogue in the imperial parliament and in Australia, of laying upon the table of the house a so-called white paper containing schedules which were tedious to read, hard to listen to, and conveyed little information when they were heard. I am sorry, however, that I cannot continue my congratulations to the point of extending them to the government in respect of the policies which have been indicated to-day by its Minister of Finance.
I should like to take this opportunity of joining with the minister in paying tribute to one who has now gone from the service of this country and to whom the minister referred, the late Hon. Mr. Sedgewiek. I concur in all that was said by the Minister of Finance with regard to that most estimable gentleman. When the tariff board was first appointed I felt that if that quasi-judicial body were left without political interference we should begin to have something like a scientific tariff at the end of five or ten years. I sincerely trust that when this government chooses a successor to the office of chairman of the tariff board it may choose one with the same high qualifications that were possessed by the late lamented chairman of that body.
I wish to make just one or two comments to-day, Mr. Speaker, while they are in my mind. As I listened to the early part of this budget address I could not help but be struck by the fact that eveiy time we have a decline in the physical volume of business in this country the minister ascribes it to world conditions; but every time trade improves he ascribes it to the marvellous powers of the present government in the matter of the negotiation of trade agreements.
The next thing that struck me was one sentence with respect to public spending. The minister said:
We dare not, we cannot, contract our expenditure until our industries and our people generally are 'spending more freely.
In large measure I agree with that statement, but the thought that crossed my mind was this: How on earth can you expect pri-

vate industry and individuals to risk their capital and venture into private enterprise when year after year this government presents a fiscal and economic policy of uncertainty affecting the conditions under which such industries will have to operate? This was brought to my mind perhaps more forcibly than usual by the fact that just before I entered this house to-day a gentleman was telling me of the results of one change in one tariff item, plus this contemplated removal of the excise tax. As a result one industry in this country employing 300 men, with an annual payroll of $297,000, will have to close its doors when this change becomes effective, unless, by some juggling of other tariffs such as we have seen in the past, that industry is given relief from the results of the Canada-United States trade agreement.
I have just one other word of comment at this time. As I listened to the minister's long dissertation upon the problems with which the government were confronted and the necessity for expenditure, I fully anticipated that when he reached the proper point he would announce a deficit somewhat similar to the deficit of 1938, which amounted to some $17,000,000. I must confess, however, that when he announced a deficit of $30,-
666,000,	together with another estimated $25,000,000 for wheat-and I hope I am not giving away any great secret when I venture to suggest that the sum required for this purpose may be considerably larger-resulting in an overall deficit of $55,666,000, the thought came to my mind that this affords the taxpayers little prospect for some years to come of any relief from the burden of taxation.
It is not possible for me, Mr. Speaker, not having had an opportunity to examine in detail the schedules and figures filed to-day, to deal at further length at this time with the budget. I therefore move the adjournment of the debate.

maintopic: AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE TORONTO ISLAND AND MALTON AIRPORTS
speechtext: How is it that Toronto has to pay for its own airports at the island and at Malton, in respect of the purchase of equipment, site, and maintenance, while other municipalities through which the same trans-Canada system passes, have these identical landing fields and airports built at the expense of all the people of Canada? There is one policy for the city of Toronto, a city which pays a great amount of taxes, and a different policy for other places. Is there a policy applying to the whole country, and if so, why is there different treatment in different localities? Some localities have to provide and maintain a national service at the expense of the local taxpayers.

maintopic: AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE TORONTO ISLAND AND MALTON AIRPORTS
speechtext:
The Department of Transport has followed a policy of assisting municipalities on the route of the trans-Canada air lines to bring their airports up to a standard. It has not been the policy of the department to build airports for municipalities wholly at the government's expense, except in cases where airports have been required for reasons other than that of serving the particular community to which it may be adjacent.
I have in mind the airport at North Ray. North Bay is a junction point in the service from Montreal to Winnipeg and from Toronto to Winnipeg. An airport in that locality was required. The city was not in a position to take any part in financing the construction of the airport, and the government decided it should be built and operated at government expense for reasons other than its service to the city of North Bay. The federal government has made a larger contribution to the airports at Toronto than it has made to any municipal airport in Canada thus far. I believe the arrangement made, a mutual one involving Toronto, the federal government and the provincial government, has worked out reasonably to the satisfaction of all concerned.

maintopic: AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE TORONTO ISLAND AND MALTON AIRPORTS
speechtext: I am not objecting to the principle of the bill. But is the city of Toronto on a branch line from North Bay, or is it on the main line?

maintopic: AUTHORITY TO CONSTRUCT AND OPERATE TORONTO ISLAND AND MALTON AIRPORTS

However, I trust Montreal will not make an issue of this, as Toronto has been disposed to do.

maintopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
I understand that the bill has been distributed. It is my intention to move, after the bill receives its second reading, that it be referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization, so that discussion need not necessarily take place at the moment with regard to it.
By way of explanation I might say that the present Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act was enacted in 1923. It is deemed expedient to reenact it, incorporating certain changes which experience in administration and changed conditions, particularly in transportation and marketing methods, have indicated as desirable. Generally, certain definitions throughout the act have been amended to meet such changed conditions, and provision is made for an advisory committee composed of representatives of an industry to assist in measures dealing with the marketing of any particular product.
With respect to the first part of the bill, under the present act the department has exercised jurisdiction over stockyard operations through the live stock exchanges, but owing to there being an insufficient number of operators to constitute an exchange, live stock exchanges do not exist at six of the eleven stockyards throughout Canada, and on that account administration of the act has not been entirely satisfactory. It is apparent that to exercise proper supervision at all stockyards it is preferable and feasible to vest greater administrative authority in the management of the stockyard. Provision is made for the continuance of live stock exchanges where they now exist, and for the establishment of others at stockyards where they may be considered feasible and desirable.
In part II there are no important departures from the present act, except for the inclusion of more desirable definitions and the clarification of the powers of the governor in council. Greater stress has been laid on the importance of grading, inspection, and branding or marking of live stock and live stock products, in order to keep step with the government's policy of assuring returns to the producer commensurate with the quality of the live stock produced and of educating the consuming public to buy by grade. In this respect it is provided that products which are below the standard of quality or grade designated on the container or package shall be deemed to be misbranded.
Part III of the bill provides that what has previously been done by regulation in connection with hatcheries and poultry in gen-

eral shall be incorporated in the provisions of the bill itself. In moving, Mr. Speaker, that the bill be now read a second time I suggest that it then be referred to the committee on agriculture and colonization.

maintopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the principle of this bill, which is now being moved for second reading, should be plain to the committee. We have a committee on agriculture, and I cannot understand why a bill of such magnitude as this should not be referred to that committee.

maintopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext: It is being referred.

maintopic: SUPERVISION OVER STOCKYARD OPERATIONS- GRADING, INSPECTION AND MARKETING
speechtext:
I am absolutely opposed to the principle of this bill, and to all these artificial barriers and burdens which are being placed on agriculture by the minister. Almost every day he introduces a new bill adding more regulations and provisos which will in my opinion only encumber the agriculture industry. It will not add to marketing efficiency and will be a restraint on the proper administration of the department.
The explanatory note says that the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act was enacted in 1923, some sixteen years ago, and that now it is deemed expedient to reenact it, incorporating certain changes that experience in administration have indicated as desirable. The bill also deals with poultry and many other agricultural activities. In my opinion the committee should know how this legislation is going to affect our export trade to the old country. There may be a scarcity of food over there in an emergency, and may not the effect of all these new restrictions and regulations be to prevent necessary reservoirs of food from being stored in England? I believe the time has come when the house should mark time on all these regulations which the minister is bringing down, because in my opinion many of them are not in the public interest.
This particular industry is also under provincial regulation. Is there any overlapping or duplication of restrictions? The minister has a small standing army of officials under various statutes and advisory boards, and by this bill provision is made for an advisory committee.	All these agencies,
inspectors and graders, and the increased number of departmental officials, are imposing an additional burden on industry at a time when there should be fewer restrictions. The Ontario legislature said a month ago that they were ready to cooperate with the dominion and, as a legislature, to strike off

Live Stock and Poultry
half the burden of taxation of their estimates or whatever other proportion might be agreed upon by all parties there, notwithstanding constitutional practice. We here should do the same.
Before we pass this bill at this late stage of the session I should like to know if the live stock industry, the stockyards and the poultry industry have been notified of the provisions of the bill and have agreed with respect to them. Who is demanding this legislation? Is the legislation necessary norw? With the session nearly over, a bill of this magnitude might well be left over until trade and commerce as represented by the live stock and poultry and other agriculture industries have a chance to be consulted. Have the views of the provincial ministers of agriculture been obtained, and if so, how many of them approve of this bill and how many disapprove?

It came before us only
now.

Because of the increasing numbers of live stock which now reach the abattoirs and packing plants direct by way of trucking, in comparison with the numbers which go to open, public stockyards, there has arisen a situation which certainly ought to be faced, and I hope

subtopic: LIMITATIONS OF POWERS OF MONEY-LENDERS WITH RESPECT TO COST TO BORROWER, ETC.

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill No. 97, respecting small loans.
He said: This is an important bill. It is substantially the one that was agreed upon by the banking and commerce committee last year, or at least by the majority of that committee. The bill has passed the Senate without amendment and now comes to the House of Commons. It stands in my name on the order paper, and perhaps I should explain briefly its provisions.
My knowledge of this bill and of its subject matter has been obtained within the last year. I have not been a member of any of the committees that have considered the matter in the last few years. I am convinced from my study of the bill and of its subject matter that a real and extensive evil exists in Canada to-day. That evil is usually called the "loan shark" business. There is a class of business known as the small loan business. It is not carried on by the chartered banks of Canada, and apparently cannot be carried on satisfactorily by them. The Canadian Bank of Commerce is engaged in this business to a limited extent, but none of the other banks has engaged in it nor have they expressed any desire to do so. In fact, the manager of one has expressed his desire to keep his bank out of it.
The need for small loans that cannot be obtained from banks is met by three classes of lenders in Canada. There are in the first place the small loan companies incorporated by this parliament under private or special acts. There are three of these companies. These companies during 1938 lent sums aggregating §9,701,658. The total loan balances outstanding due these companies at the end of 1938 was $4,764,031, and the total of interest and fees received by these three companies in 1938 was $1,096,478.
Small Loans-Mr. Ilsley

These companies do only part of the small loan business that is done in the dominion. Another part of this business is done by the provincially incorporated companies. We have not a complete or accurate record of the number of provincially incorporated small loan companies carrying on business in Canada, but a questionnaire was sent out by the Department of Insurance last year which was answered by forty-six provincially incorporated small loan companies. Therefore we know that forty-six companies incorporated by the provinces are operating. We do not know exactly how much these provincially incorporated companies lent in 1938, but we know that the amount was approximately S6,500,000 and we know the loan balances at the end of the year were approximately $3,000,000. That is the second class of lenders carrying on this business in the dominion.
Then there is a third class of lenders, that is the individual money lenders. No one knows how many of these there are. By money lenders I mean persons carrying on the business of money lending. It is perhaps fair to say, and I am convinced it is true, that the greatest abuses of money lending are found in the transactions to which these individual money lenders are parties. Indeed, the evidence given before the banking and commerce committee last year shows that the cost of loans made by some of these individual money lenders was very high indeed, running up, in some instances, into thousands per cent per annum.
May I bring before the committee some typical cases. They would be extreme cases, but there were placed before the banking and commerce committee last year instances taken from press reports of loans made by unregulated lenders, the rates for which loans amounted to over 100 per cent per annum. In one instance a loan of $45 for eight months involved a charge of 7-27 per cent a month or, converted to an annual basis, 132-1 per cent per annum. Another loan of $50 involved an annual rate of 119 per cent per annum. The lowest rate involved in a dozen or more loans dealt with was 68 per cent per annum, while one $10 loan involved an annual rate of over 91,000 per cent per annum. In the case of a loan which was reviewed by the courts in Toronto last year, the rate was found to be over 5 per cent a month, or over 80 per cent per annum.
Relief workers, persons engaged in humanitarian activities, persons who come in contact with the poor, tell of many pathetic cases of exploitation by loan sharks of persons in needy circumstances. And there has been a growing demand not only from these persons

but from all persons interested in the welfare of this country for legislation which would effectively curb what is called the loan shark evil. As I say, there is no way of knowing how much money these individual money lenders are lending in the various parts of Canada, but it is known that they are operating on quite a large scale in the cities. It is exceedingly difficult to regulate these persons; it is almost impossible to have a routine of inspection of offices when these offices are in back alleys or where there are no offices at all. For that reason among others it has been found in other countries that it is necessary to permit legitimate money lenders under the law to receive a fair return on the money they lend so that capital will enter the field and so that people in extremely needy circumstances, who cannot borrow from the banks or from others, will have a source from which to borrow some money without being thrown into the hands of these 20 per cent a month people, who inevitably operate, and operate in large numbers where there are no legitimate money lending companies which can carry on legally.
The house may be interested, and I was very much interested when I came to study this matter, in the existing legislation. I now wish to state in a few words, very simply, what the existing legislation is.
For a great many years, I think from 1858 to 1906, there was on the statute books no legislation regulating the rate of interest that might be charged. We had no usury laws. I am not sure that my historical facts are absolutely accurate; it does not make very much difference. But in 1906 the Money Lenders Act was passed. The Money Lenders Act limits the rate of interest which may be charged by money lenders on loans up to $500 to 12 per cent per annum. The Money Lenders Act has been practically a dead letter in this country. It has not been susceptible of enforcement, for this reason: If a person, a money lender, lends money and charges a rate of interest or makes, in respect of a loan, charges that amount to more than 12 per cent per annum, as most of them do, it is impossible for the courts to separate the part of the charge which is interest proper, pure interest, from the part which is taken to cover investigation of the paying ability of the borrower, documents such as wage assignments and chattel mortgages-there are usually such documents-expenses of trips to make investigation, expenses for registration of documents, and that sort of thing. So that prosecutions which have been held under the Money Lenders Act, in the comparatively﻿APRIL 25, 1939
Small Loans-Mr. Ilsley
small proportion of cases in which any evidence could be obtained, failed because the courts decided that, there being no limit on the amount that could be charged for other services and expenses, violation of the Money Lenders Act could not be established. Therefore the law is in a most unsatisfactory condition so far as regulation is concerned. That is true under both sections 6 and 7 of the Money Lenders Act. The principle of the two sections is slightly different, but both sections are continually evaded or avoided, and this can be done legally.
The house may be interested in the rates that are being charged at the present time. Apart from what I have told the house, I do not know what rates are being charged by individual money lenders. All sorts and kinds of rates arg being charged. Serious exploitation is going on.
Nor with regard to provincially incorporated companies can I tell the house with any definiteness what rates are being charged. All sorts of practices, perfectly legal practices, exist, which are authorized usually, I think, under the provincial legislation under which the companies operate. In the case of one company whose loan contracts were analysed by the department of insurance, a company in my own province, the rate of interest, including costs of loan, was found to be something over 50 per cent per annum.
Apart from the Money Lender's Act there is no check or regulation of these companies. We do have a clause in our Loan Companies Act which limits the rate which can be charged to 2J per cent per month. If I remember correctly, that provision was inserted in 1934, but it applies only to dominion incorporated companies, so there is no effective regulation of the rates charged by provincially incorporated companies, which rates are, in a good many instances fairly high.
I now come to dominion incorporated companies, which lend about $10,000,000 a year. Under their acts the charges on loans, including all costs, are as follows:

Of the loans made by these companies, 7 per cent in number, or 17 per cent in amount come between $350 and $500. That is a very small end of their business. Above $500 there
is no regulation whatever; and the bill I am presenting, as I shall explain in a few minutes, provides that instead of these rates, which on 83 per cent of the money loaned are 2 per cent and over a month, running up to 21 per cent, the maximum cost of the loan shall be 2 per cent a month.
Perhaps I should say something about the bill itself. I want to disabuse hon. members of any mistaken ideas they may entertain on this point. The 2 per cent a month is not a limitation on interest; it is a limitation on the cost of the loan. The only act on the statute books which limits the rate of interest is the Money Lenders Act, and that remains; we are not repealing thAt act. If the present bill passes and any borrower within the range of $500 from any loan company, dominion or provincial, or from any individual money lender, is able to show that the interest proper, the pure interest that is being charged, is over 12 per cent per annum, he will be able to invalidate the transaction. But he will not be able to show that, or they have not been able to show it in the past, because it is impossible to distinguish interest proper from the other charges that are also made against the borrower.

speechtext: Oh, no; court action is absolutely possible under this measure. That is why we are passing it. This bill defines the cost of a loan to include everything, all the expenses of the loan. It proVides that every contract must show on its face what the charge is, and that charge for all purposes, no matter if it is a loan of only $10 or $20 for a week, must not be and cannot be at a rate of more than 2 per cent a month, not calculated or paid in advance.

speechtext:
They might, but I do not think so. I do not have any faith in that; I think if it had been, possible the Money Lenders Act would have been invoked in the past. I do not think that is an effective way; I believe we are just deceiving ourselves if we think the Money Lenders Act is any curb on this sort of thing. That is why we must have an act that is a curb, and that is why this legislation is being introduced.
Small Loans-Mr. Ilsley

Hon. members may say to 'themselves, as would be very natural, that 2 per cent a month seems like quite a lot, and they may wonder if it would not be possible to make it less than that. Hon. members should remember that we are not talking about a loan of a thousand or fifteen hundred dollars on a mortgage. We may be and are talking of loans of $50 and SI00 for a short time, a few months; and universal experience in this small loan business has shown that if by law you deny the right to charge as much as 2 per cent a month in the case of these small loans, no one will legally make loans. That has been the universal experience. Hon. members who followed the proceedings before the banking and commerce committee must have been convinced of that. State after state of the United States union has tried to get this rate down to 1| per cent or 1 per cent a month, and the universal experience has been that the lending companies have folded up and left the state; they would not bother with it. Then the loan sharks have moved into the state, anl the business has gone on to a 20 per cent a month basis. So really we are doing harm rather than good if we make the rate too low, no matter how good a speech we may make on the subject or what an appeal we may make to people who do not understand the situation. The fact is that we will just be making the situation worse rather than better if we do not make this percentage sufficient.

That is taken as the standard of reasonableness in that country in regard to loans of this class. I think this measure is the most severe of any of the laws I have read, with the possible exception of the Wisconsin law. It must be remembered that if this bill passes the house, as I hope it will, it is not necessarily final. It is something to adopt and work under, so that if there are any abuses under it they can be corrected in future. However, it is a severe act, as acts go, having in mind the experience of other countries. Not only are we putting this provision in the bill, but we are putting similar provisions in the criminal code, so that it will be a criminal offence for the enforcement of which the attorneys general of the provinces will have some responsibility. They will have responsibility if more than two per cent is charged by money lenders in the provinces. Therefore we get the benefit of the supervision [DOT] which the attorneys general will give in connection with the enforcement of the law, and the supervision which the department of insurance will give.

The limit is set at $500. Over that amount there is no regulation. Some hon. members might think we should have stopped at $400 or $300, but if we had, there would have been no regulation over that amount. We thought that $500 was a logical maximum, because it is the maximum in the Money Lenders Act. We are allowing the Money Lenders Act to stand beside this measure, for what it is worth, and we are leaving the limit at $500.

Small Loam
Lawyers in the house will be interested in the constitutional basis of the legislation. They will say, "Are you passing legislation that you have the power to pass?" All kinds of opinions have been given during the past few years, but the Department of Justice is satisfied that this legislation is within our jurisdiction.
I shall not read any opinions, but will state briefly the two grounds on which the Department of Justice advises we have jurisdiction. Experience has shown it is impossible to try to control pure interest or interest proper unless the same authority at the same time has power to control and regulate additional charges. Therefore this legislation is legislation ancillary to interest legislation, necessary to the proper enforcement of interest legislation. That is the first ground.
The second ground is that this is criminal legislation. We are making it a crime. We say there is nothing-

speechtext: It is a crime, all right.

We are making it a crime under this legislation, and we have powers under the provisions of the criminal code. I know we cannot make everything a crime, but I think we can make this a crime, and that it will stand in the courts. So on those two grounds we consider we have the constitutional authority to pass this legislation.
For the first time the legislation brings under control all classes of money lenders. It includes not only dominion companies, but provincially incorporated companies, and individual money lenders. It brings the real charges out into the open, so that he who runs may read, and so that no one may say to the borrower, "You are to be charged seven per cent"-or be charged ten per cent, or twelve per cent. There must be a statement of exactly what is to be charged. He is charged that much, no more and no less, not in advance and only on the outstanding balance.
We believe the rate is high enough to permit the legitimate money lending company to live and to carry on, but we do not think it is too high, or so high as to permit them to derive undue profits, in the light of the experience of such companies elsewhere, and in view of what others have found out to be practical in this line of business. It provides for control by the attorneys general, in discharging the responsibility of enforcement of the criminal law, and it provides for control by the superintendent of insurance.
It does not raise the interest rate now chargeable. Under the Money Lenders Act the rate now chargeable is 12 per cent, and it will remain the same. Finally, I would say 71492-202

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING APPOINTMENT OF SECRETARY OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Before speaking on this bill I should like to read the text of it in order that it may :be placed on the record. Section 1 reads:
Section three of the Civil Service Act, chapter twenty-two of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, as amended by subsection two of section thirteen of chapter forty of the statutes of 1932, is further amended by adding at the end thereof, the following subsection:
"(9) The secretary of the commission shall be appointed by the governor in council."
That is the proposed amendment. We always look to the explanatory note to ascertain if possible the reason for amendments of an act. The explanatory note to this bill reads:
The position of secretary to the civil service commission already exists under the civil service classification. The purpose of this bill is to

provide that the appointment of the incumbent thereof shall be made by the governor in council.
It seems to me that this is another bill to take away powers of the civil service commission, the appointment in this case being that of the secretary of that body. The two civil service commissioners and the chairman are appointed by the governor fn council; and now it is proposed to deprive the commission of the power to select its own secretary from the civil service. At the present time there are, I believe, two acting secretaries of the commission-

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING APPOINTMENT OF SECRETARY OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext: Why two?

subtopic: AMENDMENT REQUIRING APPOINTMENT OF SECRETARY OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION BY GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
-the English secretary and the bilingual secretary. Formerly we had one secretary, Mr. Foran, who has since retired. This particular amendment has impressed upon me the fact that we are raising in this dominion a racial question. Probably the English-speaking people themselves have been more or less to blame. There is no doubt that we have forced upon French-Canadians certain appointees who could not speak the language of the people with whom they had to do business. The result is that the people of Quebec now feel that they have not been fairly represented in the civil service of Canada. I have often wondered what these commissioners do, and whether their main duty is to see that when an appointment is made either a Frenchspeaking or an English-speaking person is appointed, as the case may be, losing sight of the chief object, namely, the actual merits of the person receiving the appointment. This has caused more trouble in the service than anything else, and it will continue to do so unless some remedy is found.
If there is at the head of an organization someone who is constantly urging something in particular to the disadvantage of others, it is bound to cause friction, and that is what I contend with regard to the commissioners themselves. It must be admitted that the English-speaking citizens of Canada have refused to adopt any of the customs of the French-Canadian. We have more or less refused to learn their language, but they have not refused to learn English. It stands to reason that when an appointment is made in Quebec, the French-Canadian suffers from the fact that in the past we attempted to force upon him English-speaking persons who could neither speak nor understand his language.
I suppose this explains the presence on the order paper of a couple of bills this year and one last year. With Bill No. 3, introduced

Civil Service Act
a year ago, I agreed in principle. I did feel that we should not ask the French-Canadian to do business with an English-speaking person through an interpreter. The bill was passed. This year, however, I notice that an attempt is being made to convey to the civil service commission, not merely the idea that we are in favour of the bilingual principle, but that the person appointed must be a French-Canadian as well. I want to be fair, because I think we are losing something in drawing a straight line of distinction whereby, for example, I would not endorse the appointment in my district of a person who happens to speak my language unless that person was English as well. And the same principle would apply throughout the province of Quebec. It would be most ridiculous; for I know that in the London district the engineer is a French-Canadian, and so far as I am concerned I must say that as long as that man does his work properly he will remain there. After all, if we box ourselves up we cannot have unity. If I am not willing to learn the customs of my neighbour and he is not willing to learn at least some of my customs, I cannot be friendly with him, and I shall not be able to improve my mind-because no one can say that any one race has all the brains in the country.
I feel that is what these bills imply. I still say that we were to blame in the past and we probably brought this on ourselves, but I do think the sponsors of these bills should bear with us and realize that we are making a great mistake in attempting to carry our remedy too far. Even in Ontario, where there are a great many French-Canadians, to say that no one but an English-speaking person should be appointed is unfair. I repeat, we are losing the benefit of intermingling, the benefit of the other man's ideas, and we are certainly not promoting unity in Canada.
I do not think we should appoint commissioners simply to say this is an English appointment or that is a French appointment, and allow that to be the guiding principle. They should be able to get together and assist in the endeavour to bring about goodwill among the different races in Canada. I think that is a part of their duties in view of the large number of appointments which must be made in the service from day to day, and they can put that idea into practice if they so desire. I do not believe, however, that we should take any action which would tend to a greater division among the races. I know the sponsor of this bill very well, and I do not believe that he has this in mind.
I do not understand why the secretary of the civil service commission, whose duty is 71492-202J
now purely secretarial, should be appointed by the governor in council. We all know that a secretary sometimes assumes the duties of the whole commission and advises and more or less controls same. We were informed in committee that the only duties of the secretaries at present acting are secretarial; that the commission now formulate their own program and administer the act. I cannot agree with the suggestion that the commissioners themselves should be appointed from the service, because, after all, while you are in a service which is dealing with all phases of life you sometimes get in a rut and continue in that rut. I think it is an improvement to bring in new blood, new ideas, into any commission. Although I agree with the principle of promotions within the service, the merit idea, yet I believe that the appointment of the commissioners themselves should remain with the governor in council, the government in power; because, after all, the government is responsible and must answer to the people within a reasonable time. Therefore we should not attempt to confine these positions to one particular class of people.
Further, while it is satisfactory to have two secretaries, one English and one French, one bilingual secretary would do. We must realize that large sums of money are spent on government services. It appears ridiculous to have two secretaries to do only secretarial work, in other words take dictation from the commissioners, type the letters, probably mail them, and take telephone calls. One salary could be saved. And I would say to our English-speaking ptopulation that if we refuse to learn the French language and thus equip ourselves for bilingual positions it is our loss. We are losing something in life. On the other hand, if a French-Canadian is willing to become bilingual and is capable of filling the position there is no reason why he should not receive the appointment. And if an English speaking person who is bilingual applies there is no reason why he should not receive it. We must try to get away from this idea of always saying one is French and another is English; there is too much of that to-day.
For these reasons I cannot support this bill.

I wish to speak briefly in opposition to this bill. I listened to the hon. member (Mr. Lapointe, Matapedia-Matane) who moved the bill, but I could not learn much from him because he spoke in French. However, I read his speech in Hansard carefully, and with all due regard to the hon. gentleman I must say that he failed to convince me that there is

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very short bill, containing only this sentence:
The secretary of the commission shall be appointed by the governor in council.
The explanatory note does not do much more than repeat that sentence in a different way. It states:
The position of secretary of the civil service commission already exists under the civil service classification. The purpose of this bill is to provide that the appointment of the incumbent thereof shall be made by the governor in council.
While -the bill does not contain anything else, the speech made by the mover and the circumstances under which the bill was introduced permit us to see that what was in the mind of the mover was that certain qualifications should be possessed by the secretary of

Civil Service Act
the commission. But, as has been pointed out even in editorials published by newspapers which favour my hon. friend's point of view in this matter, the bill would not actually bring about that result. It is quite easy to imagine a government not having unanimous views about the qualifications that should be possessed by the secretary of a commission, so the mere transferring of a position from one to the other would not, in a statutory way at least, cure the evil or bring about the result my hon. friend has in mind.
I have looked through all the acts and amendments concerning the civil service commission, and I have been impressed with the fact that there is no mention of the secretary in any of them. Apparently it has not occurred to anyone, since the inception of the commission, to suggest any change in the position of the secretary. I attribute that situation largely to the fact that the gentleman who occupied that position until last year had done so from the beginning, and apparently there was no desire to change his status or to dispute his jurisdiction in the least. If hon. members turn to the act as it appears in the revised statutes of 1927 they will find set out in section 3 how the commission is to be appointed by the governor in council; how the chairman is to be appointed, the tenure of office and everything else concerning the commissioners themselves, but they will not find a word about the secretary. I have carefully read through the civil service regulations and find the same situation; they contain nothing concerning the appointment, the qualifications or the-work of the secretary.
It was only in 1932, when a special committee was appointed to study the operations of the act, that a recommendation was made in this connection, part of which was read by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), suggesting that the work of the secretary be lightened and that the executive duties be transferred to someone else. This recommendation, however, was not acted upon; and when the previous government brought in amendments to the Civil Service Act, which were assented to May 26, 1932, nothing was done about changing the status, the method of appointment or anything else concerning the secretary.
Last year the committee dealt extensively with the secretary of the civil service commission. I am not going to act as arbiter between the chairman and the secretary, or express the least opinion as to the sittings of the committee which dealt with that question. I have in my hand, however, the report of the committee which sat last year, as it
appears in the votes and proceedings of June 29, and I find that in that report there is a recommendation embodying and endorsing the recommendation made by the committee of 1932. I will not read it, because the hon. member who preceded me has done so. I will point out simply that in the report the committee recommended that the secretary of the civil service commission be called upon to perform only those duties which are peculiarly those of a secretary.
Since that time the secretary of the commission, who had acted as such since the first days of a civil service commission in Canada, has been superannuated. I can inform the house the commission of to-day have taken action on the recommendation of last year's committee and have recommended a separate position to take care of the executive part of what had been the customary, if not the statutory, duties performed by the former secretary. The commission have also recommended that two joint secretaries be appointed to deal with the correspondence. That is the situation at the present time.
This year the sittings of the special committee on civil service matters have been revived. I understand from the chairman that this committee held its last sitting this morning, and that the report is almost ready and will be available in a few days. Had the debate on this bill been resumed at an earlier date it was my intention to suggest that the subject matter of the bill be placed before the special committee. However, the committee having completed its work, there will be no purpose in such reference. I understand, further, from the speeches I have heard to-night, that the position of secretary was discussed both this year and last year, and that, therefore, there would be nothing further upon which that committee could report.
Under those circumstances and with the expectancy that the whole Civil Service Act may be up for discussion at some time during the present session, may I say I feel we are serving no useful purpose in extending the debate to greater lengths. I would suggest that as the sponsor of the bill has attained his end of creating a discussion occupying some reasonable time, he might be willing to withdraw his bill.

subtopic: LIMITATION OF POWERS OF MONEY-LENDERS WITH RESPECT TO COST TO BORROWER, ETC.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley for the second reading of Bill No. 97, respecting small loans.

subtopic: LIMITATION OF POWERS OF MONEY-LENDERS WITH RESPECT TO COST TO BORROWER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the minister in charge of the bill upon his clear-cut presentation of the case for second reading of this bill. As hon. members are aware, this matter occupied the attention of the banking and commerce committee at several meetings extending over a period of two sessions, and I think any person who endeavoured to follow the proceedings of that committee will agree that most unremitting and earnest attention was given to the problem.
The situation which confronted members of the committee-or so it seemed to me- was this: Many of us felt that a rate of two per cent a month, an effective rate of 26J per cent per annum, was too high to ask people who wished to borrow small sums of money to pay. We knew that those who borrowed more than $500 or perhaps $1,000, $1,500 or more, could get money at 6 per cent or 7 per cent per annum, and to say that those who wished to borrow smaller sums should have to pay an effective rate of 26J per cent per annum was felt by many members of the committee to be unfair. That, I believe, was the cause of much of the difficulty experienced in the committee.
Those who felt that some legislation should be passed argued first of all, as the minister pointed out this afternoon, that, with the law as it stood, private money lenders could charge any rate they wished, and get away with it. It was pointed out that provincial companies could charge any rate they wished and get away with it, and that dominion small loan companies were actually charging, in many instances, up to 2i per cent a month. While in one decision it was suggested they had no right to do so, in another decision their right was upheld, and so there seems to be considerable doubt as to the legal effect of their charter in that regard. In any event it must be admitted that if it were found they did not hare the right to charge the rates they are charging they could cease to do business as a dominion company, incorporate as a provincial company, and then go ahead and charge any rates they wished. So it was pointed out to those of us who felt that a rate of two per cent was exorbitant, that if we stopped the legislation going through by arguing about it further we were actually permitting people to exploit unmercifully those who needed small sums of money, and
[Mr. A. J. Lapomte.)
that there would still be no control over them whatsoever.
I must admit that the thought that this parliament might be drawing to a close, that it might now be in its last session, that we had spent two sessions wrestling with the problem and that if we did not pass some measure we would actually be leaving a bad situation no better than it was before, had a great deal to do with the attitude I have decided to take towards this bill.
In that connection it should be remembered that shortly after assuming office the present attorney general of Ontario found this was such a crying evil in this province that he decided to bring to court some people who were charging exorbitant rates of interest, rates which, I believe, amounted to over 50 per cent per annum. They were brought for trial before His Honour Judge O'Connell presiding at the county court judge's criminal court of the county of York. When acquitting those charged, this is what Judge O'Connell had to say:
These harsh and inequitable transactions might be effectively dealt with, if not actually stopped, by legislation making it a criminal offence, with appropriate penalties, to charge, impose or collect in respect to a loan for less than $500, interest, and for services of any kind, nature or description whatsoever in connection therewith, a sum of money amounting in the aggregate, in respect to both interest and charges, to more than two and one-half per centum per month on the monthly balance owing by the borrower. This, of course, is merely a suggestion prompted by the evidence coming before me during the present trial.
So the judge-who had the opportunity to consider these cases, although it was proved beyond doubt that these people were charged more than 50 per cent per annum, found he could not do anything under the law as it stood, and suggested that the law be amended by making it a crime to charge such rates, just as is suggested by the government to-day, except that the judge suggested two and a half per cent while the government sets an overall rate of two per cent. My attitude was in the committee, and still is, that two per cent a month is too high a rate to charge, but I took the attitude that we must be realistic and that it was better to prevent charges of over 50 per cent per annum-as the minister has pointed out it sometimes amounts to 1,000 per cent-than to continue arguing about the matter indefinitely.
Furthermore, if at this session we pass this bill and the companion amendment to the criminal code setting a roof of two per cent a month, there is nothing to prevent us from carrying on our campaign for lower rates of interest from now on. At least a step forward will have bee*- taken.

Small Loans-Mr. Tucker
There is another point which should be considered by this house. I argued strongly before the committee that some of the provinces were very much interested in the development of credit unions and cooperative credit institutions, and that if these small loan companies were permitted to go into a province and charge two per cent a month they might, by a program of advertising, get such a hold on the province as to prevent the credit institutions from experiencing that development of which I believe they are capable. I am quite satisfied that the full possibilities of cooperative credit institutions have not been exploited to anything like the extent they should be. There seems to be the idea that credit unions can flourish only in urban communities, but I am satisfied that they can operate successfully in farming districts as the people become more cooperative-minded.
Coming from Saskatchewan, where we have just passed a credit union act, I wanted to see it given every chance of success, and I did not want to see these loan companies coming in and perhaps hindering the development credit unions might otherwise have. So I, with some other members, took the attitude that if the provinces were given some say in the matter I would not have nearly the objection to this bill that I was expressing at that time. The suggestion was made in many different forms that we should set a top roof of two per cent and say that one per cent should be counted as interest and the balance as a service charge for all other items included in the two per cent, which would enable the province, if it desired, power to prohibit the last mentioned one per cent.
That in effect is what this bill accomplishes; for I wish particularly to draw to the attention of the house the fact that the bill introduced by the government to-day is different from the bill recommended by the banking and commerce committee in one particular that is important from that point of view, and that is that this bill, as pointed out by the minister, does not repeal the Money Lenders Act, as the bill recommended by the committee did. I rather gathered from what the minister said that he did not think that was of any great importance, but to me it is of great importance, for this reason: The dominion by this bill is not authorizing two per cent a month as interest. It is leaving a top roof as interest pure and simple of 12 per cent per annum, and it is saying that the top roof for all charges, including interest, shall be two per cent a month. In other words, 12 per cent is interest, and the balance of two per cent a month covers all other charges to the borrower.
Somebody may say, the minister did say, that you cannot distinguish between interest and other charges, but here is the essential point as I see it. The province, if it sees fit, can. after this bill is passed, prohibit money lenders from making any other charge than the interest charge authorized by law under the Money Lenders Act. Charges for investigation, drawing documents, and so forth, certainly come within provincial jurisdiction, under the heading, in section 92 of the British North America Act, of "property and civil rights within the province," and so, after we have passed this bill, with the Money Lenders Act left in existence the province will still be left in full charge of the situation, to the extent so many of us urged before the committee. In other words, I am satisfied that the province, after this bill passes can, if it wishes, prohibit any other charges outside of interest, and the Money Lenders Act declares that the interest can be only 12 per cent per annum. So the province of Quebec, for example, which is interested in the development of the caisses populaires, could, after this bill is passed, prevent these loan companies from operating and charging two per cent a month. It would only need to pass a law, within its jurisdiction under property and civil rights, prohibiting them from making a service charge for drawing documents, making investigations and so forth, or any other charges except the 12 per cent interest under the Money Lenders Act. Then the Money Lenders Act could be enforced. The reason why it could not be enforced up to now was that when cases of exorbitant charges were brought into court the defendants said: We are charging only 12 per cent interest, and the balance is for our trouble in making investigations, drawing documents and so forth. The county court judge would say:	I cannot differentiate between these charges; perhaps 40 per cent of the 50 per cent may be for service charges and so forth, and the other 10 per cent for interest, I cannot distinguish between them. But with the Money Lenders Act and this bill in force, the province controls the situation. So one reason that has moved me to think we should acquire control of the situation to the extent that this bill will enable us to do has been the fact that the minister and the government have seen fit to take out of the bill the provision repealing the Money Lenders Act.
Another reason is this:	Some of us argued
strongly before the banking and commerce committee that the making, of exorbitant charges against needy boiTOwers certainly
Small Loans-Mr. Tucker

should be made a crime. We argued that while the superintendent of insurance sitting here in Ottawa might think he could control this evil throughout the length and breadth of Canada, on the other hand at least an alternative control would be a good thing. After all, the administration of justice is committed to the province. They have the police force under their control; they have- their attorney general's department with its law enforcement officials and so forth. With the charging of over two per cent made a crime even a private citizen seeing the law being broken might not bother to let the superintendent of insurance know, but he might tell a policeman who could lay a charge. A good many loan sharks, private individuals, do business in small offices or from their homes and so forth, and we argued: How in the world could the superintendent of insurance enforce the law?
Therefore I felt it to be a powerful reason why I feel I can support the minister in urging the second reading of this bill, that he proposes to make it a criminal offence to charge more than two per cent interest to the borrower. The effect of that as stated is this: If any one of us knows that in our town or village or community anybody is charging more than two per cent a month interest, we do not have to write to the superintendent of insurance or anybody else. We can either go ourselves and lay a charge against the person who did it or bring it to the attention of a law enforcement officer, and it may be said that man is -breaking the law no less than if he were breaking into a store and the law set in motion. I am satisfied that by putting such a provision into the criminal code we are doing more to control this evil than could be done by any other single means, because it will then be the duty of every policeman from one end of this country to the other to lay a charge if he knows that the law is being broken. This will ensure more complete enforcement than leaving it to an official in Ottawa no matter how efficient. So I commend most highly the minister and the government for being willing to write this into the criminal code of the country.
Personally I should like, however, to see the height of the roof which we are putting on, which makes it a criminal offence, put lower than two per cent a month. But, we had witnesses, including some experts from the United States, appear before our committee, and the minister has so well indicated the situation they outlined that I will not

do any more than mention it. They argued that if you are going to have legitimate companies in the field at all you must let them charge even more than two per cent a month; thus the experts wanted the rate put higher than that now proposed, but the superintendent of insurance said that the rate must be reduced to two per cent a month if he was to recommend the bill, and that is the form in which it comes before us. The suggestion is that if we are to let them go into the business at all we must allow them to charge two per cent a month.
In that regard, let me say that the reason why I support the bill is not that I believe we should let them charge two per cent a month. But the s:tuation is that to-day they are charging that much, and more. Provincial companies are charging more than that. Private companies are charging more than that. The reason why I am supporting the bill is that it cuts down the rate which is being charged, and I look to the time when it will be again cut substantially. In his report for the year ended December 31, 1937, the superintendent of insurance said this:
The experience of the companies up to date shows that a flat monthly rate of 2 per cent is an adequate rate to yield a fair profit to the lenders. The two companies which applied for legislation at the last two sessions of parliament accepted the amendments made to their bills to provide for such a rate. The report of the committee in 1938 included a draft bill providing for that rate.
I do not think that is quite correct. I believe that the draft bill had the rate in blank.
It is therefore to be hoped that some means will be found of making such a rate effective for the companies generally. Should it be later found that a lower rate is justified the legislation can be modified accordingly.
Therefore I suggest to this house that, now it is agreed by everybody that we should bring the rate down to two per cent, we should not argue and oppose the bill because we would like to get the rate down to one per cent-as I personally should like to do-but we should all agree to give at least this measure of lowered rate, and those of us who want to lower it further can continue our agitation to have it lowered. I concluded that was the proper attitude for me to take.
There is one thing in this bill to which I should like to draw the minister's attention. The first part of the bill would indicate we are providing that no one can charge more than two per cent a month. The second part of the bill seems to indicate that these companies may charge two per cent a month. I

Small Loans-Mr. Tucker
should like to have it made perfectly plain that when we say these dominion companies may charge two per cent a month we are giving the power to charge it only if it is within the law of the province where they are doing business to make that charge. I think that the proper place to have that section which provides that they may make that charge is in the private bills themselves instead of in part II of this bill, in order to make it plain that the general law of the land, both provincial and dominion, shall apply to these companies, and that the special act of incorporation which says they may charge that amount gives them the power to charge it only if it is otherwise legal to do so. However, I will bring up that point when the bill is in committee.
With regard to the question of preserving provincial jurisdiction, I think everybody who is studying the trend of affairs to-day realizes that more and more the tendency is for big corporations, trusts and combines secretly to get together to control the economic life of this country. They do not do it in such a way that one can definitely prove that they are in a trust or combine. That has happened especially, I believe, in regard to the farm implement industry, and as I see it the only hope of contending against the trend towards trusts and combines getting a stranglehold of the people of our free democracies, and especially Canada, is by throwing more and more our weight and strength behind the development of cooperative institutions along all lines which will enable the people to band together and protect themselves against exploitation by cartels, trusts and combines. So, Mr. Speaker, I am one hundred per cent behind the idea of credit unions.
I have a suggestion to make to the government. I remember that when I made it last year, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was good enough to applaud it, and I hope he feels about it the same way to-night.
Good work is being done in developing credit unions in Quebec and Nova Scotia; credit union laws have now been passed, I believe, in every province of Canada; and in the United States there are credit union laws in almost every state. President Roosevelt, with his consuming interest in such matters, saw to it that a credit union law was passed for the whole of the United States, and it has been found useful in that country. In other words, there is great development under both state and federal credit union laws, and I suggest that the government should give serious consideration to setting up a federal credit union law for this country. I also
suggest that serious consideration be given to an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act which will enable the central credit union organization in each province to use the Bank of Canada for rediscount purposes and put the Bank of Canada behind the cooperative banking institutions as it is behind the commercial banks of this country. Giving them the right of rediscount in the Bank of Canada should be helpful. I have not time to enlarge upon that, but it is something which should be considered.
There is another matter. We all know that in order to make the people conscious of what can :be done along the line of cooperation, a great deal of education is necessary. I suggest in all seriousness that this year we should have had an appropriation to pay at least two men, one in the east and one in the west, to educate people along the lines of cooperative credit. Or the money that that would require could be given to the Canadian association for adult education, which is doing great work along that line, to help them further. After all, when the government is giving these companies the right to charge two per cent a month, it is not asking too much to suggest that it should put at least ten thousand dollars in the estimates to develop cooperative credit institutions and foster the support of them throughout the country.
There is another matter with which I should like to deal before I conclude. I do not wish to take more than sufficient time just to cover some of the important points. It was brought out before the committee that one of our banks, the Canadian Bank of Commerce, had seen fit to set up a department to deal with the so-called small loans. Evidence was given by their representative that during the twenty months from June, 1936, until the time the evidence was given they had made small loans to the extent of 18,800,000. That was in addition to the small loans which they made in the ordinary course of business. To indicate how important is the action of one bank, I should like to compare the $8,800,000 lent by this one small loan department with the amount that all three federal small loan companies lent in 1937; the total amount of their loans that year was only $10,410,000. In other words, in twenty months one bank in its small loan department lent almost as much as these three companies lent in 1937, the last year for which I have figures. This indicates to me definitely that if the other banks had entered the field, as this one did, there would not be very much

Small Loans-Mr. Tucker

demand from small loan companies for this money that is costing 26i per cent per annum interest.
Someone may say, however, " Oh, but these people who are borrowing this money are not creditworthy; there is too big a risk, and so the rate must be high." Well, according to the figures given the committee the losses of the small loan companies on loans of $28,919,000 during four years amounted to only $41,873, or -14 per cent, a little over one-tenth of one per cent. What does that mean? It means that the people who are paying this high rate of interest are really creditworthy; they are repaying their loans.
This brings me back to something I suggested at the opening of my speech. We have given the chartered banks of Canada valuable privileges on the understanding that they will handle the credit requirements of the Canadian people, and that does not mean just the Wealthy people; it means not only the rich but those of more limited means. And what have we before us to-day? We have one bank trying to meet the situation while the other banks have failed to do so. The average rate charged by the Canadian Bank of Commerce was 10-5 per cent per annum, much less than borrowers have to pay to the small loan companies.
From my place in the House of Commons I feel impelled to say this. If the banks are not prepared to live up to the obligations resting upon them as a result of the special privileges they have been given by the people of Canada, as set out in the Bank Act and in the Bank of Canada Act, then if it is my privilege to sit in this house when the banks come for a renewal of their charters I will say to those that have not entered this field and supplied credit to poor people who are creditworthy, "You have not discharged your responsibility to the Canadian people and do not deserve a renewal of your charter."
If the banks could be persuaded to enter this field; if credit unions were fostered, I personally do not believe that there would be any need for this high interest money. I support this measure, but I do so in order to bring under control those people who are charging all over the country far higher rates than 26i per cent. I support the bill in order to get something in the criminal code which will indicate to these people who are exploiting the needs of their fellow men to the extent of, in many instances, as high as 100 per cent per annum that they will be put into gaol if they continue. I do it also in the hope that the legislature of the province from

My hon. friend is a lawyer, and I am not, but I question that. Invading the sacred precincts of law, I suggest that there is without doubt a question in the minds of many whether by translating the word "interest" into "costs" this parliament can acquire jurisdiction over transactions of this sort. Parliament's right to control is limited under the

Small Loans-Mr. Stevens
British North America Act to the control of interest rates. That is pretty generally accepted. I am aware that the Department of Justice officials have a fairly comfortable conviction that they may be able to sustain this, but it is not by any means certain. That, however, is not particularly what I wish to emphasize. What I emphasize is this. We are saying to the people of Canada that companies are justified in charging 26J per cent interest on small deserving loans. That is my first point. I know there is a danger that one will be charged with being prejudiced against certain individuals because one questions certain principles, but I can assure these companies that I am not questioning their transactions as they are carried on, so far as we know. I do question, however, the justice of their charging 26| per cent to a very large proportion of their borrowers.
My hon. friend has quoted the percentage of losses-I believe he said [DOT] 14 per cent, or a little more than one-tenth of one per cent. Look at Ottawm. Many, I venture to say most, of the borrowers are civil servants with permanent jobs who, through sickness or because of operations in the family or through some misfortune or another, find themselves forced to borrow $300, $400 or $500. They have a permanent job; they have assurance that they can pay; there is no question about it; yet they are charged 26i per cent; and parliament by this legislation is saying that this is a fair and just rate of interest; for as sure as we pass this legislation it goes out to the country that we are approving this rate of interest. My hon. friend reminds me that the advertising of these companies bears the legend "under the supervision of the dominion government." That is something to which I distinctly object. I want to make it clear that I am not supporting this legislation, because I cannot bring myself to justify the charging of 26J per cent to deserving, safe borrowers.
In the second place, if the amendment to the criminal code presently before the house [DOT] in another bill is passed-which by the way is the method that I have advocated for years-and if we maintain the Money Lenders Act as it is at present with its limit of 12 per cent, then I think there is no need of this legislation at all. We have these three companies; they are carrying on under private charter, there is no reason why they should not continue to carry on. But all that the minister told us this afternoon about loan sharks, provincial companies and so forth, will be controlled and controlled only through the criminal code, not through this bill.

So I rose simply to make my position clear, because I have taken a strong stand on this matter for years. I am not disposed, to try to block the legislation, but simply say that parliament in enacting it gives its sanction to a rate of interest of 26J per cent, which I believe to be unnecessary.
I entirely agree with the statement of the hon, member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) that the banks of Canada ought to follow the example of the Canadian Bank of Commerce and inaugurate a small loan system or department. I think the wisest thing would be for all the banks to join together and set up a small loan bank if you like, or company, financed by all the banks, so that it would have the experience, direction and control of the banking fraternity of this country and the financial strength that is inherent therein, and set up small loan organizations in all the different centres of Canada so as to make credit available to deserving people at the more reasonable rate of interest charged in the case of the Canadian Bank of Commerce.
It may be said that the Canadian Bank of Commerce will lend only under an endorsement, and that these small loan companies lend on chattel mortgages and such collateral security. There is no difficulty for the banks to work out a similar system to that of these small loan companies, occupy that field and advance the moneys at a much lower rate of interest. As a matter of fact, the largest company operating now in this class of selected loan companies under dominion jurisdiction obtains its money abroad. The last time I saw its statement the company had some $6,000,000 borrowed from the parent company in the United States. There is no reason why there should not be, under the direction and control of the chartered banks, a subsidiary small loan concern which could borrow its funds from the banks. As already pointed out, this class of business, generally speaking is reasonably safe, as evidenced by the sum of $28,000,000 lent in a period of four years with a loss of only about $40,000, a phenomenally low rate of loss.
So I am by no means satisfied that this legislation is a step in the right direction, because I feel that parliament, having enacted it, will wash its hands of the responsibility which we owe to the small and needy borrower.

Under my 1935 proposal the banks could handle loans up to $500. There might be an assignment of wages for security or as a consideration, or there might be security of some collateral of another kind. It could be handled by the province or by the municipalities, or by agencies like the Red Cross, the banks and insurance companies, as trustees, with the guarantee of the government at three per cent or less. The Minister of Finance said the other day the government can borrow money for two-thirds of one per cent. If so, why do they not act here?
The loan companies charging high rates are not the companies that are referred to on the back of the bill. Hon. members would be surprised to hear the rates that some of the old companies are charging and of the way they foreclose at will. They got high rates in good times and should reduce rates. Some of these companies charge $4,000 for a loan of S6.000 for ten years. Then, with respect to private mortgages, some of our most respected citizens are charging $4,000 for a loan of $6,000 for ten years. I know one loan company that has charged up to $6,000 for a loan of $9,000 for nine years. So I say that all these companies should come under proper regulation and the better class of mortgage companies as well. Does anybody know of anything that we have attempted to do in this parliament to control these companies? You make regulations and appoint boards to deal with telephones, insurance policies, real estate mortgages and the gasoline tax, but there is no real regulation at all of any of them. They are a law to themselves. If a private citizen has a complaint to make he is told to see the attorney general of the province because the enforcement of all federal law is entirely on the provinces, and the government replies to any complaints made here: "No information." Regulation is non-existent.
Under this bill it is proposed that the superintendent of insurance shall regulate these companies, but no regulation, human or divine, can control these loan shark people, the way they do their business, because they adopt a policy of secrecy, and it is impossible to check them up by any system of inspection.
I believe that the present bill should start off with a rate of one, not two, per cent. That would get rid of some of these companies and wind them up. They no doubt have, a few of them, vested rights, and something might have to be done along that line. But undoubtedly parliament should step in and give the industrial worker a break, and take this whole business of personal loans for the future over to the chartered banks. It may be needed

for only two or three years. Wages might be assigned as security. These borrowers can offer just as much security as there is behind some of the loans that have been made to federal harbours and to bankrupt provinces, one of which owes from fifty to sixty-five million dollars which will never be paid back. Why not set up a fund of five or ten million dollars to be loaned to industrial workers on the security of an assignment of their wages, in much the same way that assistance was given to farmers under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act and to fishermen when the act was extended to them in 1935 by the late government? This new policy can be handled by the banks for the government who guarantee it.
In conclusion, I believe that this legislation will not be a success if the bill is passed. You will not be able to have proper inspection. This means that we shall be back to where we started because there is no way of regulating these people and their shark methods. This form of personal loan is in its infancy in Canada and is unregulated, and we should try to keep it in infancy and not encourage its growth along the lines indicated by the bill. I urge that consideration be given to our industrial workers in the large cities, where unemployment is the greatest, and that they be given the same fair treatment as has been given by the federal government to the farmers and fishermen of this country, and others. Let us take this matter over and end this shark system, and let us nationalize this small loan business in the public interest and of the industrial workers who are suffering so much.
