speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the minister (Mr. Usley) stating it was his desire that this bill should pass; but I wish that the government would carry out their promise to issue currency and credit in terms of public need, and I would also remind the house of the Prime Minister's statement that "usury, once in control, will wreck any nation." There are many thousands throughout the length and breadth of this country who are in receipt of what we have called deficit incomes. In a period of financial stringency they find themselves in need of a comparatively small amount of money to meet some emergency, and they are forced to pay 26-8 per cent interest for that money if this bill passes. In other words, we are giving the sanction of parliament to a rate of 26 per cent interest.
I have in my hand a pamphlet issued by one of these small loan companies. This particular one is issued by the Central Finance

Small Loans-Mr. Landeryou
Corporation, and at page 4 I find this under the heading "Is there a real need for cash credit?"
We all know about the credit facilities which are available in connection with the purchase of goods. We refer to this as "instalment buying." The need for this service is readily recognized. But many of us fail to realize another need and the problems involved in meeting it. This is the need of the consumer for a source of cash credit to meet emergencies like sickness, accident, death, temporary unemployment and entanglement in debts that demand immediate payment.
Our own experience proves that there is a real demand for cash credit. During the last four years, Central Finance Corporation in the province of Ontario alone, made 86,204 loans, totalling $15,213,781. The business has increased from less than $1,500,000 annually to more than $6,250,000 in four years in one province. Such a demand should be equally well supplied in the other provinces.
These small loan companies fasten themselves upon some industrial area where there is a large population and loan to needy borrowers money-for what purposes? I find from page 245 of the banking and commerce committee report, No. 5, that they loan money to meet expenditures as follows:
The purposes of borrowing are given as medical, dental and hospital.
The number of customers of the Central Finance Corporation is given as 4,459, who borrowed money to pay overdue bills. What does that mean? It means that there are thousands and thousands of people who borrow money or desire to borrow it to meet overdue bills. They are people with deficit incomes, who have been encouraged through advertising and high pressure salesmanship to purchase on the instalment plan goods which industry produces and is unable to sell for cash. So the goods are sold on the instalment plan of a dollar down and a dollar when they can catch the fellow at home. These people with deficit incomes are unable to meet the payments as they fall due; they get behind in their commitments; the loan shark company comes along and says, "I will come to your rescue," and it loans him the money at from 24 to 26 per cent interest. The position is simply this, their last state is worse than their first. That is the evidence which was given by a witness before the banking and commerce committee: they are far worse off after they get the money than they were before they borrowed it. How can we allow these loan shark companies to loan money at 26 per cent interest to these people to meet overdue accounts on instalment purchases? Many thousands of people in this country buy a table and a few chairs,
a bed and some blankets, and some needed household utensils, on which they have to pay 12 per cent interest because the goods were bought on the instalment plan. Then, because they have not enough money to meet their payments on the due dates, they are harassed; the loan shark companies claim them as their victims, and the government will not do anything for them except pass a bill legalizing a rate of interest of 26 per cent.
Who else borrowed and for what purpose? The report shows that 1,766 customers borrowed to pay arrears of taxes. Many people are afraid of losing their homes because their taxes are in arrears, and in order to pay those taxes they are forced to become victims of these loan sharks and pay 24 or 26 per cent interest on the money they borrow.
Again, 1,529 borrowed money to buy fuel. Not having been able to secure during the summer sufficient salary or wages to buy their winter supplies of fuel, they became victims of these loan companies. Yet parliament is sanctioning a rate of 26 per cent, permitting these sharks to loan money to people who need fuel to keep themselves warm in winter. It is outrageous.
It also appears that 1,745 borrowed money to meet real estate mortgages and interest. Others borrowed to pay their insurance. All these were needy borrowers, but their credit was good. Evidence has been given before the banking and commerce committee that less than one per cent of all the money that these companies have loaned is lost; at least that represents the arrears carried on their books, it may not be lost." These people are suffering from deficient incomes; they are being robbed of a decent wage in industry or a decent income as primary producers and forced to become victims of these loan sharks. The government says that there is no alternative, that if we do not pass this bill these people will be forced to have recourse to private loan sharks who will lend them money at rates of interest as high as 1,000 per cent.
With such a state of affairs, nothing is done. The minister suggests that nothing can be done. Why, the government is going to the moneylenders and borrowing at less than half of one per cent. I know that many citizens can borrow from the banks at 6 per cent. Yet these deserving citizens, for whom no provision has been made except through the loan department of one commercial bank, and who are forced to become victims of usury, receive no consideration from the government. speechtext:
While I am not enthusiastic about this legislation,
I hope it is the beginning of better legislation to be brought in by this parliament or the next. I think we are agreed that the Money Lenders Act has failed miserably to correct the abuses of the loan sharks. I regard this bill as a measure of legislation, thinking that a half loaf is better than none. Any one of us who has known anything about the activities of loan sharks in our cities realizes the need of some effective legislation along this line. We have in our midst a vicious octopus that has been bleeding the industrial workers of our cities. I do not like 2 per cent a month interest any better than any other hon. member, but if the passage of this legislation will be the means of putting out of business the man or the company that is getting 100 per cent or 90 per cent or 200 per cent or 50 per cent, then I must support the bill.
I have asked myself several questions. Is there a need? There is. Have the banks satisfied this need; are they prepared to take care of it? Evidently not. Are the borrowers good risks? I think the evidence before the

committee proves that they are. If my memory is right, the number of people who did not make good their loans was one-tenth of one per cent. Will such legislation curtail the activities of the loan sharks and partly correct the abuses that we find to-day? I think the answer is that it will. For these reasons I support the bill.

subtopic: LIMITATION OF POWERS OF MONEY-LENDERS WITH RESPECT TO COST TO BORROWER, ETC.
speechtext:
Like others who have previously spoken, I am not wildly enthusiastic about this legislation. Reference has been made to the evidence adduced before the committee that the rate of interest prevailing in Great Britain is 3 per cent, 3J and 4 per cent a month. But I point out that in Great Britain there are conditions prevailing that we have no desire to duplicate here; they have had a relief roll, or a large number of people on the dole, for a long time. It was pointed out also that many of the states of the United States have rates varying from 2i per cent to 4 per cent, and the officers of the Russell Sage foundation in giving evidence stated that a company could not function at a lower rate of interest. Again I point out that at the present time they have some 11,000,000 unemployed in the United States and a condition there that we have no desire to perpetuate in this country.
I cannot understand the abundance of propaganda to which we have been subjected during the last three years, when those who were sponsoring three private bills for the amendment of already existing legislation, differentiating themselves, levelled broadside after broadside against what they termed the loan shark. So far as I am concerned I see no difference except in degree between the business carried on by these people and some others whom they condemn in such strong terms. We are told that the people responsible for this propaganda carry on a business that is beneficial to the needy and the poor. A Mr. Bunce, I do not know who he is-

subtopic: LIMITATION OF POWERS OF MONEY-LENDERS WITH RESPECT TO COST TO BORROWER, ETC.
speechtext:
Thank you.
Mr. Bunce, describing the small loan operations as "a business that helps the poor, the needy and the distressed," also warned against fixing too low a maximum interest rate on small loans as this would encourage monopoly and would deprive scattered population areas of service.
When we turn to the booklet issued and widely circulated by the small loan companies, we find that in 1935 the Central Finance Corporation loaned to 23,897 borrowers a total of $4,227,713, and that the average monthly income of these borrowers was $145, or an average yearly income of over $1,700.

Small Loans-Mr. McNiven
This is the class of customer that favoured the Central Finance Corporation; yet one witness before the committee referred to the customers of these small loan companies as the poor, the needy and the distressed.
Just in passing, may I say that I was surprised to find editorials appearing in leading newspapers across the country, and to find copies of these editorials coming to my desk in almost the same mails. In one of these editorials I found this declaration: "Control the salary buyer and the loan shark." Those who are alleged to charge anywhere from 30 to 700 per cent were described as salary buyers. What I say to you, Mr. Speaker, is that in 1935 the Central Finance Corporation had 23,987 customers, each a salaried man in receipt of an income averaging $145 a month. Why should men in that position be compelled to go to a loan shark and pay 2, 2i or 3 per cent a month? I have a special regard for those groups of men who find themselves in difficulties and who honestly desire to pay their obligations, and in order to do so find their way to the loan shark.
A moment ago some reference was made to the Canadian welfare council, and I find here a reference to the evidence of Miss Charlotte Whitton:
Experience of the Canadian weltare council a workers, the committee was told by Miss Charlotte Whitton, director, showed that all charitable and philanthropic resources "do not in the present circumstances prove adequate to the need and, therefore, you are left wholly to the consideration of the commercial field. . . . Short term borrowing over a very broad stratum of low income families and individuals is extensive and will continue."
Then they go on to quote Mr, Dobson, president of the Candian Bankers' Association, who-
-told the committee that he believed "small loan companies would always find a field in which to operate, since there was a class of borrowers which the banks .	.	. could not
reach, though banks might well advertise more extensively the service they are prepared to offer borrowers."
I	should like to join in the request that was made by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) and others who have spoken, and to ask the minister and the government to bring special pressure to bear upon the banking system of this country in order that they may enter that field and follow the lead which has been established by the Canadian Bank of Commerce, which I
believe is entitled to our deepest gratitude for the work it has done. As the hon. member for Rosthern pointed out, that bank loaned more than these three loan companies put together, and at an interest rate less than half that charged iby these companies. I do believe that the banks of this country should get together and canvass the situation. If even a fraction of the money they spent on that useless series of advertisements that they published in the newspapers of this country last year could be spent in catering to this kind of investment they would do far more to perpetuate their position and obviate criticism than could be done by all the advertising of that kind they could carry on for the next ten years.
The banks have gained experience during the last three years. Only this afternoon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) told us that under the home improvement plan some 65,000 borrowers had obtained from Canadian banks unsecured loans repayable within three years, and that the loss on loans exceeding $26,000,000 was only $19,000. On a previous occasion I mentioned a conversation I had with a bank manager in Saskatchewan, who told me that the banks had overlooked a profitable field of investment which was made known to them through their experience with the home improvement plan. He told me that his branch had made three-quarters of all the loans in a city of 60,000 people; that there had not been a single default; that they had not lost a dollar; that every borrower had met his payments as and when they matured. I think, if some pressure were brought to bear upon the banks, they would realize this problem, and I believe that in view of the consideration they have received from the people and from parliament they might enter this field and make a contribution to the solution of a problem that is a cankef upon the body politic.
The other phase of the matter which I should like to develop for a moment has been touched upon already; that is, the credit unions. I was glad to hear the eulogy of Mr. MacDonald, and I should like to add a word in praise of Mr. Desjardins who, I think, first introduced la caisse populaire in the province of Quebec. I understand that now there are some 371 credit unions in that province, and that the loss in the operation of those unions is almost negligible. Not
Small Loans-Mr. Blackmore

long ago I ran across an item in a local paper which stated that because of the legislation introduced by various states of the union fixing the rate of interest at 2( per cent per month and up, the federal government of the United States some two years ago adopted a general law for the formation of credit unions. Since then, some hundreds of credit unions had been formed, and I think they loaned some $13,000,000 to their members, with a loss of only $1,070.
I was going to say that at the last session of the legislature of Saskatchewan a credit union bill was passed. Since then, some twenty-two credit unions have been formed, and they are functioning profitably to-day. A minute ago an hon. member referred to the class of individuals who receive loans from these companies. I was particularly interested in the number of civil servants. Out of a total of 23,987 borrowers there were 4,462, or 18 per cent, civil servants. We owe the civil service one of two duties, either to pay them a remuneration sufficient to render it unnecessary for them to appeal to loan companies or, second, to provide them with a facility which will make it unnecessary for them to go to a loan shark for assistance.
The next largest group was the group connected with the manufacturing industry, to which reference was made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), and which comprises 11-47 per cent of the total. I found that 4-93 per cent of the borrowers were engaged in banking, insurance and real estate businesses. We find that 9-7 per cent were engaged in the retail trade.
I happened to be in the committee one morning when one of the witnesses was giving evidence. He was asked if the Canadian Bank of Commerce was interfering with their business and, as I recall it, his reply was, "They sure are; they have already taken 191 of our customers." All through the evidence they indicated, and in their literature they advertise that their service is an emergency. Yet we find the representative of one of the companies stating the bank has taken 191 of their customers.
This brings me to my conclusion, and it is this: Once an individual finds himself in the hands of these small loan companies, life for him is a continuous chain of emergencies. It is just one emergency after another until he succeeds in getting out of their hands, or out of their clutches. Far better would 
it be for a borrower tempted to go to one of these companies to go to his creditors and state the facts. Any man who is in receipt of a monthly income of $145 can talk business to his creditors on a basis which would not require him to go to these companies.
I am somewhat disappointed in the legislation. I am more fearful about it than I was before I saw the bill. I notice that according to paragraph (f) of section 2 a small loan company is described as a company incorporated by special act of parliament, and authorized to lend money on promissory notes or other personal security, and on chattel mortgages. I anticipate now that there will be a flood of applications for registration under this measure. Then we shall have the question of vested interests, just as we had with those companies which were corporated in 1928 and 1929. We shall be told that because they have a dominion charter and have made investments, therefore they ought to be privileged to continue operations. We shall then be told that they cannot function at two per cent, and we shall be asked to raise the rate to 2J per cent or to three per cent.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we use our ingenuity and our ability to further the cause of the credit union, and in the meantime exert the maximum of pressure upon the banks to serve this field.

subtopic: LIMITATION OF POWERS OF MONEY-LENDERS WITH RESPECT TO COST TO BORROWER, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not feel disposed to accept this bill. I see many things about it which are entirely as they ought not to be. It is high time now-the monetary knowledge and experience of the world is sufficient to enable people who so desire, to know and understand -that this dominion government created money and used it to help these people who need it. If the government do not propose to do the lending themselves, then certainly they can support the banks, as has been suggested by two or three hon. members, so that the chartered banks of Canada can engage in this small loan business, and enable the people to keep out of the hands of all kinds of small loan companies.
It is a significant fact that the people who borrow these small amounts are already more or less poor. When they procure a small loan they become poorer. What we want in Canada is a means whereby we may enable people to become better off. Certainly we

War Munitions
shall not do it by passing laws like this. If the law were necessary, it would be a different matter; but it is absolutely unnecessary. If we think it is necessary, then I say our thinking needs to be readjusted.
There is another important matter which I believe is involved, and that is the question of where the money going into these loans is coming from. A great deal of it comes from across the line. Already we pay too much interest on money coming from outside this country. It is high time we began to realize that money which we need in Canada can be originated here, and that the interest can be paid to Canadians, instead of to people across the line.
